h1: Whisky in Indian weather and serving temperature
title: Serving Whisky in Indian Heat | Craft Beer School
desc: How Indian heat changes the way whisky smells and tastes, the serving temperature to aim for and how to store bottles through summer.
teaser: Room temperature means something else in Chennai in May. Here is how to serve whisky when the room is 32 °C.
standfirst: Most whisky advice assumes a cool room. In an Indian summer the same pour smells hotter, sharper and more alcoholic. A few small changes fix most of it.
sections: Room temperature was never meant to be 32 °C

Tasting notes and distillery guides tell you to drink whisky at room temperature. That advice was written for rooms in Scotland, Ireland or Kentucky, where indoor temperatures sit somewhere around 18 to 22 °C for much of the year. A flat in Chennai, Nagpur or Delhi in May can sit at 30 to 35 °C even with a fan running.

That gap changes the whisky in the glass. Ethanol evaporates faster as it warms, so a warm pour sends a stronger wave of alcohol vapour up your nose. The finer aromas, such as fruit, flowers and malt, get pushed behind the burn. Many people who say they find whisky too harsh are really drinking it too warm.
Aim for 18 to 20 °C in the glass

For tasting a whisky neat, a pour at around 18 to 20 °C is a sensible target. Cool enough to tame the alcohol, warm enough for the aroma to rise. Below about 12 °C most whiskies close up and taste of little except sweetness and alcohol.

You do not need a thermometer. If the bottle feels slightly cool in your hand, close to the feel of water from a clay matka, you are in the right range. If it feels warm, it is too warm for careful tasting.
Ways to bring a warm pour down

There are several ways to cool whisky. Each changes it differently:

  • A splash of cool water. Lowers temperature and alcohol together. For most whiskies this is the best first move.
  • One large ice cube. Melts slowly, chills fast and dilutes gradually. Good for an evening drink, less good for careful tasting.
  • A chilled glass. Keep the glass in the fridge for 15 minutes. It cools the first few sips without adding water.
  • Keep the bottle in a cool cupboard. An interior cupboard away from outside walls can run several degrees cooler than the room.

Our guide to whisky on the rocks covers what ice does in more detail.
Why the fridge is not the answer

Keeping whisky in the fridge seems like an easy fix for Indian heat. It cools the whisky too far. At 4 to 5 °C most aromas stay locked in. The whisky tastes thin and sweet. Some unfiltered whiskies may also turn slightly hazy when very cold, which is harmless but puzzling the first time.

Bottles taken out of a fridge also sweat in humid air. Labels peel, corks get damp and the outside of the bottle drips. A cool cupboard does the job better than the fridge.
Storing bottles through an Indian summer

Heat does not ruin a sealed bottle overnight, but it does slowly work on it. Keep whisky:

  • Upright, so the spirit does not sit against the cork and soften it.
  • Out of direct sunlight. Light fades colour and can dull flavour over months.
  • Away from the kitchen stove, the top of the fridge and outside walls that bake in the afternoon.
  • Out of a parked car. A car interior in summer can reach temperatures that push the cork and damage the spirit.

An opened bottle with a lot of air in it loses aroma faster in heat. If a bottle is less than a third full and will not be finished soon, pour the rest into a smaller clean bottle.
Heat in the warehouse is a different story

Indian heat also matters long before the whisky is bottled. Casks in hot warehouses lose spirit to evaporation much faster than the roughly 2% a year often quoted for Scotland. The whisky also takes flavour from the wood more quickly. That is why a young Indian single malt can taste older than its age suggests.

That is a production question, covered in our guide to temperature swings in Indian warehouses. In your home the goal is simpler: slow the heat down once the whisky is yours.
Highballs are the hot weather answer

When the room is properly hot, a long drink often makes more sense than a neat pour. A whisky highball, about 30 to 45 ml of whisky topped with three or four times as much chilled soda over plenty of ice, stays cold and refreshing for longer. It also spreads one measure over a whole glass, which suits a slow evening.

Use a tall glass filled to the top with ice so the cubes melt slowly. Pour the whisky first, stir once to chill it, then add soda gently down the side so the bubbles last. A light, fruity blend or a grain whisky works better here than a heavily sherried malt. Save the expensive single malt for a cooler evening and a tulip glass.

Pour the same whisky into two glasses, about 15 ml each. Leave one at room temperature. Stand the other in a bowl of cool water for ten minutes. Nose both, then taste.

Most people find the cooler glass smells of more than alcohol: fruit, honey or cereal come through that the warm glass hid. Once you notice that, you start judging whisky by what it smells of rather than by how much it burns. Drink water alongside and keep the pours small. That one test will change how you serve whisky through the hot months.
faqs: What temperature should whisky be served at?
For tasting neat, around 18 to 20 °C works well. Warmer than that and the alcohol dominates; much colder and the aroma closes up.
Is it bad to keep whisky in the fridge?
It will not harm the whisky, but it serves it too cold to taste properly. A cool cupboard is better.
Does heat damage a sealed whisky bottle?
Long exposure to heat and sunlight can damage the cork and dull the whisky over time. Store bottles upright, out of the sun and away from heat sources.
Why does whisky taste harsher in summer?
Warm whisky releases more alcohol vapour, which masks the finer aromas. Cooling it slightly or adding a splash of water helps.
